name: Janine Makorre
intro: This website documents my contributions to the Wiki Education Claim-Source Verification Library project during the Outreachy October 2026 contribution phase.
about: I work across product and service design, UX research and technology, with experience in data science and document processing.

contributions.title: Claim Verification — Issue #7037
contributions.summary: The starting point: 10 claims from the exercise and 10 independently selected Wikipedia claims, each investigated against its cited material.
contributions.problem: A citation can be relevant to the topic without supporting the exact statement beside it. Wording, context and access to the full source change what can be concluded.
contributions.approach: Recorded the exact claim and citation, retrieved the source, located passages in context, and wrote a human assessment before documenting separate AI comparisons.
contributions.outcome: A report with claim records A01–A10 and B01–B10, evidence locations, written reasoning, access notes and reflections. The report is a contribution to review, not an independently adjudicated benchmark.
contributions.lesson: Locating the relevant passage could take longer than assessing it. Matching a keyword was only the beginning; reading around it mattered.
contributions.limitation: Assessments reflect the contributor's interpretation. This portfolio does not certify every verdict as correct. Some records would benefit from more precise excerpts or a second review.
contributions.ai: I wrote the human assessments and documented later ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini comparisons separately. AI also assisted planning, research into unfamiliar concepts, formatting and editing, as disclosed in my report.
contributions.task: Independently assess whether 10 claims from the Dashboard exercise and 10 additional Wikipedia claims are supported by their cited sources.
contributions.myContribution: I recorded the exact wording and citation for each claim, located and read the source, and documented my assessment with relevant passages and evidence locations. I recorded later AI comparisons separately from my human assessments.
contributions.result: My report contains 20 claim records, source-access notes, written explanations and reflections. Recurring challenges included locating relevant passages, handling partial support and distinguishing inference from what a source explicitly states.

preview.work: I read sources, located relevant passages and recorded my human assessments before separate AI comparisons.

contributions.title: Comparing Claim Verification Assessments — Issue #7175
contributions.summary: A qualitative comparison of seven public contributor reports, looking beyond verdict labels to the evidence and reasoning behind them.
contributions.problem: Different articles, verdict vocabularies and interpretations make a single agreement percentage misleading. Even overlapping claims can be assessed differently.
contributions.approach: Compared recurring patterns across seven reports and examined overlapping claims where possible: partial support, qualifiers, numerical context, missing evidence and human–AI reasoning.
contributions.outcome: A synthesis of concrete examples and open questions for annotation guidance: retain subclaims, exact passages, locations, explanations, limitations and reviewer disagreements.
contributions.lesson: Agreement does not establish ground truth. A useful reference assessment needs an evidence trail and a documented review process.
contributions.limitation: This is a qualitative synthesis, not a formal reliability study or validation of every contributor's conclusion. Suggested data fields and a pilot remain proposals.
contributions.ai: This portfolio summary was drafted with Codex from my research report. The original contributor reports remain linked through that report.
contributions.task: Review publicly shared contributor evaluations and report recurring patterns in their assessments and reasoning.
contributions.myContribution: I reviewed seven contributor reports, compared overlapping claims where possible, and examined partial support, qualifiers, numerical context, disagreement and uncertainty. I used a qualitative comparison because the reports covered different articles and verdict labels.
contributions.result: I documented examples of both agreement and disagreement, along with questions for clearer annotation guidance. The report proposes recording exact passages, locations, reasoning and unresolved differences; it does not independently validate every assessment.

preview.overview: Compare publicly shared claim assessments and reasoning.
preview.work: I reviewed seven contributor reports and examined recurring patterns and overlapping claims.
preview.outcome: A qualitative comparison covering partial support, disagreement, uncertainty and evidence traceability.

contributions.title: Improving the Verify Claim Experience — Issue #7151
contributions.shortTitle: Improving the Verify Claim Experience — Issue #7151
contributions.summary: A student experience that keeps the claim, source passages and reasoning together—and introduces AI only after an independent judgment.
contributions.problem: The local walkthrough exposed nested scrolling, source evaluation before source reading, a verdict accepted without explanation, and loss of an unsaved edit on refresh.
contributions.approach: Revisited an initial Figma direction after inspecting the existing exercise. Focused the redesign on evidence traceability, independent judgment and optional reflection.
contributions.outcome: A Figma Handoff connecting Understand the Claim → Evidence Workspace → Make a Judgment → Compare with AI → Completion, with optional expanded reading, reasoning review and independent practice.
contributions.lesson: The existing exercise already offered five nuanced verdicts and source-access distinctions. The design opportunity was to make the evidence and thinking easier to follow.
contributions.limitation: Proposed design, not a shipped Dashboard feature or student usability study. Saving, highlighting, verdict changes and AI responses are illustrative. Educational, accessibility and student validation remain necessary.
contributions.ai: I developed the initial UX direction and guided the refinements. Codex assisted technical inspection, later screen refinements, content checks and design-screen QA.
contributions.task: Suggest improvements to the student verification experience, focusing on ease of use and evidence-evaluation skills.
contributions.myContribution: I developed an initial Figma design and refined it after reviewing the local walkthrough. I focused on keeping claims and source passages together, documenting reasoning, and introducing AI comparison after an independent judgment.
contributions.result: I produced a UX case study and a linked Figma Handoff with an Evidence Workspace, an optional expanded reader, judgment and AI-comparison screens, completion, optional reasoning review and a separate practice challenge. These are proposed designs, not implemented Dashboard features.

preview.overview: Propose improvements to the student verification experience.
preview.work: I developed and refined a Figma proposal informed by the local walkthrough.
preview.outcome: A UX case study and UX Flow Designs. These are proposed designs, not implemented features.

contributions.title: Local Dashboard Exploration
contributions.summary: An AI-assisted local walkthrough with a fictional student account and sample claims, used to reconsider the initial UX proposal.
contributions.problem: Designing from assumptions risked proposing features already present and missing friction that only appears through interaction.
contributions.approach: Explored article selection, highlighted claims, citations, source access, assessment, saving and revision in a local development environment.
contributions.outcome: A screenshot-supported review identifying what to preserve—context, five verdicts, source-access distinctions and revision—and where the workflow could become clearer.
contributions.lesson: An assessment saved without an explanation in the tested flow. A separate refresh check removed unsaved text while retaining the previously submitted response.
contributions.limitation: Synthetic account and locally seeded exercise. Not production research, a live student study, or independent verification of the selected sample claim. The temporary test response was removed.
contributions.ai: Codex assisted local setup, the walkthrough, technical inspection and documentation. I reviewed the findings and used them to identify design priorities.
contributions.task: Explore the existing claim-verification flow locally before refining the UX proposal.
contributions.myContribution: With Codex’s assistance, I explored a local Dashboard installation using a fictional student account and sample claims. I reviewed claim selection, citation access, assessment, saving and revision, and documented the observations with screenshots.
contributions.result: The walkthrough identified nested scrolling, source evaluation before source reading, a verdict accepted without an explanation, and an unsaved edit lost on refresh. It also identified features to preserve: article context, five verdicts, source-access distinctions and revision of submitted responses.

preview.overview: Run and review the existing Dashboard verification exercise locally.
preview.work: With Codex’s assistance, I explored the flow using a fictional student account and sample claims.
preview.outcome: A screenshot-supported walkthrough identifying existing strengths and areas for improvement.

contributions.title: Style Guide Initialization — Issue #4465 / PR #7204
contributions.summary: Merged two-commit contribution restoring standalone style guide React initialization and correcting DatePicker date bounds.
contributions.problem: The standalone entry point failed because I18n was not initialized before dependent components loaded; examples also needed Redux context.
contributions.approach: Investigated startup dependencies, initialized translations early, supplied a small Redux store through Provider, and added regression tests in English and Spanish. Parsed DatePicker bounds as dates and tested inclusive limits and out-of-range input.
contributions.outcome: PR #7204 was reviewed and approved by Sage Ross (ragesoss) and merged into WikiEducationFoundation/WikiEduDashboard master on 29 October 2026. Two commits restore initialization and correct date-bound handling. Focused validation passed 42 tests on Windows and Linux with zero date-fns warnings.
contributions.lesson: The public website was not a verified baseline. A controlled original-versus-patched comparison was necessary to attribute differences to the patch.
contributions.limitation: Addresses part of Issue #4465. Popover positioning, missing component examples and wider style guide work remain outside scope. The merge does not establish deployment or shipped Evidence Lab designs.
contributions.ai: Codex assisted implementation, tests, validation and PR preparation. I selected the issue, questioned assumptions, directed the controlled comparison and reviewed the scope and results.
contributions.task: Investigate and restore existing React examples that were not rendering on the standalone style guide page.
contributions.myContribution: I selected the issue, reviewed the investigation and directed a controlled original-versus-patched comparison. Codex assisted with the two-file implementation, regression tests and validation. The patch initializes translations before dependent components and provides the required Redux context.
contributions.result: Merged upstream as PR #7204 after review and approval by Sage Ross (ragesoss). Two commits restore standalone React examples and correct DatePicker bounds, with regression coverage for date limits.

contributions.title: Outdated Code Comments — Issue #6871
contributions.summary: Examined stale mixin terminology and date-handler documentation, then withdrew a cleanup patch whose practical value was not established.
contributions.problem: Old terminology can mislead developers, but a wording change alone does not necessarily fix a substantive problem.
contributions.approach: Inspected InputHOC and DatePicker behavior and reassessed the proposed edits against mentor guidance to prioritize consequential inaccuracies.
contributions.outcome: No code committed, pushed or submitted for this issue. The proposed work was archived and the investigation branch returned to its original clean state.
contributions.lesson: Both date-handler branches return ISO timestamps. An early proposed explanation would have introduced a new inaccuracy; further inspection caught it.
contributions.limitation: Comment-only parsing and lint checks established unchanged executable behavior, not that the wording edits were needed.
contributions.ai: Codex assisted code inspection, drafting, reassessment and checks. I reviewed the findings and mentor feedback and chose not to submit.
contributions.task: Investigate comments that no longer accurately describe the surrounding implementation.
contributions.myContribution: With Codex’s assistance, I inspected InputHOC and date-picker documentation and reviewed the proposed changes against mentor guidance to prioritize substantive inaccuracies.
contributions.result: I decided not to submit the cleanup patch because its practical value had not been established. I documented that decision in the issue discussion. No code was committed, pushed or submitted for this investigation.
